entries.454046d5b72a34b971bdfc7d525b2d45c1ac78b9: <div sID="gen6047" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="2Sam.6" sID="2Sam.6"/> <div eID="gen6047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6048" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6049" type="x-p"/> The obscurity of the ark, during the reign of Saul, had been as great a grievance to Israel as the insults of the Philistines. David, having humbled the Philistines and mortified them in gratitude for that favour, and in pursuance of his designs for the public welfare, is here bringing up the ark to his own city, that it might be near him, and be an ornament and strength to his new foundation. Here is, I. An attempt to do it, which failed and miscarried. The design was well laid, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. But, 1. They were guilty of an error in carrying it in a cart, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3-2Sam.6.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 2. They were punished for that error by the sudden death of Uzzah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6-2Sam.6.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>), which was a great terror to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8-2Sam.6.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>) and put a stop to his proceedings, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.10-2Sam.6.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. II. The great joy and satisfaction with which it was at last done, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. And, 1. The good understanding between David and his people, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17-2Sam.6.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. 2. The uneasiness between David and his wife upon that occasion, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.16">ver. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20-2Sam.6.23">20-23</reference>. And, when we consider that the ark was both the token of God's presence and a type of Christ, we shall see that this story is very instructive.
entries.c730ac91fbbfbf951d2227157f68cd93c25cae90: <div eID="gen6049" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6048" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Removal of the Ark. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen6050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Again, David gathered together all <hi type="italic">the</hi> chosen <hi type="italic">men</hi> of Israel, thirty thousand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David arose, and went with all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God, whose name is called by the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts that dwelleth <hi type="italic">between</hi> the cherubims. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they brought it out of the house of Abinadab which <hi type="italic">was</hi> at Gibeah, accompanying the ark of God: and Ahio went before the ark. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David and all the house of Israel played before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> on all manner of <hi type="italic">instruments made of</hi> fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals. <div eID="gen6050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6051" type="x-p"/> We have not heard a word of the ark since it was lodged in Kirjath-jearim, immediately after its return out of its captivity among the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1-1Sam.7.2">1 Sam. vii. 1, 2</reference>), except that, once, Saul called for it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">1 Sam. xiv. 18</reference>. That which in former days had made so great a figure is now thrown aside, as a neglected thing, for many years. And, if now the ark was for so many years in a house, let it not seem strange that we find the church so long in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.14">Rev. xii. 14</reference>. Perpetual visibility is no mark of the true church. God is graciously present with the souls of his people even when they want the external tokens of his presence. But now that David is settled in the throne the honour of the ark begins to revive, and <hi type="italic">Israel's care of it to flourish again, wherein also,</hi> no doubt, the good people among them <hi type="italic">had been careful, but they lacked opportunity.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Phil.4.10">Phil. iv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen6051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6052" type="x-p"/> I. Here is honourable mention made of the ark. Because it had not been spoken of a great while, now that it is spoken of observe how it is described (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2">v. 2</reference>): it is <hi type="italic">the ark of God whose name is called by the name of the Lord of hosts that dwelleth between the cherubim,</hi> or <hi type="italic">at which the name, even the name of the Lord of hosts, was called upon,</hi> or <hi type="italic">upon which the name of the Lord of hosts was called,</hi> or <hi type="italic">because of which the name is proclaimed, the name of the Lord of hosts</hi> (that is, God was greatly magnified in the miracles done before the ark), or <hi type="italic">the ark of God, who is called the name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.11">Lev. xxiv. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.24.16">16</reference>), <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord of hosts, sitting on the cherubim upon it.</hi> Let us learn hence, 1. To think and speak highly of God. He is the name above every name, <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> that has all the creatures in heaven and earth at his command, and receives homage from them all, and yet is pleased to dwell between the cherubim, over the propitiatory or mercy-seat, graciously manifesting himself to his people, reconciled in a Mediator, and ready to do them good. 2. To think and speak honourably of holy ordinances, which are to us, as the ark was to Israel, the tokens of God's presence (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.2">Matt. xxviii. 2</reference>), and the means of our communion with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. It is the honour of the ark that it is the ark of God; he is jealous for it, is magnified in it, his name is called upon it. The divine institution puts a beauty and grandeur upon holy ordinances, which otherwise have no form nor comeliness. Christ is our ark. In and by him God manifests his favour and communicates his grace to us, and accepts our adoration and addresses. <div eID="gen6052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6053" type="x-p"/> II. Here is an honourable attendance given to the ark upon the removal of it. Now, at length, it is enquired after, David made the motion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1-1Chr.13.3">1 Chron. xiii. 1-3</reference>), and the heads of the congregation agreed to it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.4">v. 4</reference>. All the chosen men of Israel are called together to grace the solemnity, to pay their respect to the ark, and to testify their joy in its restoration. The nobility and gentry, elders and officers, came to the number of 30,000 (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1">v. 1</reference>), and the generality of the common people besides (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1 Chron. xiii. 5</reference>); for, some think, it was done at one of the three great festivals. This would make a noble cavalcade, and would help to inspire the young people of the nation, who perhaps had scarcely heard of the ark, with a great veneration for it, for this was certainly a treasure of inestimable value which the king himself and all the great men waited upon, and were a guard to. <div eID="gen6053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6054" type="x-p"/> III. Here are great expressions of joy upon the removal of the ark, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.5">v. 5</reference>. David himself, and all that were with him that were musically inclined, made use of such instruments as they had to excite and express their rejoicing upon this occasion. It might well put them into a transport of joy to see the ark rise out of obscurity and move towards a public station. It is better to have the ark in a house than not at all, better in a house than a captive in Dagon's temple; but it is very desirable to have it in a tent pitched on purpose for it, where the resort to it may be more free and open. As secret worship is better the more secret it is, so public worship is better the more public it is; and we have reason to rejoice when restraints are taken off, and the ark of God finds welcome in the city of David, and has not only the protection and support, but the countenance and encouragement, of the civil powers; for joy of this they <hi type="italic">played before the Lord.</hi> Note, Public joy must always be as <hi type="italic">before the Lord,</hi> with an eye to him and terminating in him, and must not degenerate into that which is carnal and sensual. Dr. Lightfoot supposes that, upon this occasion, David penned the <reference osisRef="Ps.68.1-Ps.68.35">68th Psalm</reference>, because it begins with that ancient prayer of Moses at the removing of the ark, <hi type="italic">Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered;</hi> and notice is taken there (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.25">v. 25</reference>) of the <hi type="italic">singers and players on instruments</hi> that attended, and (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">v. 27</reference>) of the princes of several of the tribes; and perhaps those words in the <reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">last verse</reference>, <hi type="italic">O God, thou art terrible out of thy holy places,</hi> were added upon occasion of the death of Uzzah. <div eID="gen6054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6055" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is an error that they were guilty of in this matter, that they carried the ark in a cart or carriage, whereas the priests should have carried it upon their shoulders, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3">v. 3</reference>. The Kohathites that had the charge of the ark had no wagons assigned them, because <hi type="italic">their service was to bear it upon their shoulders,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.7.9">Num. vii. 9</reference>. The ark was no such heavy burden but that they might, among them, have carried it as far as Mount Sion upon their shoulders, they needed not to put it in a cart like a common thing. It was no excuse for them that the Philistines had done so and were not punished for it; they knew no better, nor had they any priests or Levites with them to undertake the carrying of it; better carry it in a cart than that any of Dagon's priests should carry it. Philistines may cart the ark with impunity; but, if Israelites do so, they do it at their peril. And it mended the matter very little that it was a new cart; old or new, it was not what God had appointed. I wonder how so wise and good a man as David was, that conversed so much with the law of God, came to be guilty of such an oversight. We will charitably hope that it was because he was so extremely intent upon the substance of the service that he forgot to take care of this circumstance.
entries.b78fcdc55a3a811fc6270236292eddf01dee09d2: <div eID="gen6055" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Uzzah Slain for Touching the Ark; The Ark in the House of Obed-edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen6056" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth <hi type="italic">his hand</hi> to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> And the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for <hi type="italic">his</hi> error; and there he died by the ark of God. <hi type="super">8</hi> And David was displeased, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had made a breach upon Uzzah: and he called the name of the place Perez-uzzah to this day. <hi type="super">9</hi> And David was afraid of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that day, and said, How shall the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> come to me? <hi type="super">10</hi> So David would not remove the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto him into the city of David: but David carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> continued in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> blessed Obed-edom, and all his household. <div eID="gen6056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6057" type="x-p"/> We have here Uzzah struck dead for touching the ark, when it was upon its journey towards the city of David, a sad providence, which damped their mirth, stopped the progress of the ark, and for the present, dispersed this great assembly, which had come together to attend it, and sent them home in a fright. <div eID="gen6057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6058" type="x-p"/> I. Uzzah's offence seems very small. He and his brother Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, in whose house the ark had long been lodged, having been used to attend it, to show their willingness to prefer the public benefit to their own private honour and advantage, undertook to drive the cart in which the ark was carried, this being perhaps the last service they were likely to do it; for others would be employed about it when it came to the city of David. Ahio went before, to clear the way, and, if need were, to lead the oxen. Uzzah followed close to the side of the cart. It happened that the oxen shook it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6">v. 6</reference>. The critics are not agreed about the signification of the original word: <hi type="italic">They stumbled</hi> (so our margin); <hi type="italic">they kicked</hi> (so some), perhaps against the goad with which Uzzah drove them; <hi type="italic">they stuck in the mire,</hi> by some. By some accident or other the ark was in danger of being overthrown. Uzzah thereupon laid hold of it, to save it from falling, we have reason to think with a very good intention, to preserve the reputation of the ark and to prevent a bad omen. Yet this was his crime. Uzzah was a Levite, but priests only might touch the ark. The law was express concerning the Kohathites, that, though they were to carry the ark by the staves, yet <hi type="italic">they must not touch any holy thing, lest they die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.4.15">Num. iv. 15</reference>. Uzzah's long familiarity with the ark, and the constant attendance he had given to it, might occasion his presumption, but would not excuse it. <div eID="gen6058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6059" type="x-p"/> II. His punishment for this offence seems very great (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The anger of the Lord was kindled against him</hi> (for in sacred things he is a jealous God) and he <hi type="italic">smote him there for his rashness,</hi> as the word is, and struck him dead upon the spot. There he sinned, and there he died, <hi type="italic">by the ark of God;</hi> even the mercy-seat would not save him. Why was God thus severe with him? 1. The touching of the ark was forbidden to the Levites expressly under pain of death—<hi type="italic">lest they die;</hi> and God, by this instance of severity, would show how he might justly have dealt with our first parents, when they had eaten that which was forbidden under the same penalty—<hi type="italic">lest you die.</hi> 2. God saw the presumption and irreverence of Uzzah's heart. Perhaps he affected to show, before this great assembly, how bold he could make with the ark, having been so long acquainted with it. Familiarity, even with that which is most awful, is apt to breed contempt. 3. David afterwards owned that Uzzah died for an error they were all guilty of, which was carrying the ark in a cart. Because it was not carried on the Levites' shoulders, <hi type="italic">the Lord made that breach upon us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.13">1 Chron. xv. 13</reference>. But Uzzah was singled out to be made an example, perhaps because he had been most forward in advising that way of conveyance; however he had fallen into another error, which was occasioned by that. Perhaps the ark was not covered, as it should have been, with the covering of badgers' skins (<reference osisRef="Num.4.6">Num. iv. 6</reference>), and that was a further provocation. 4. God would hereby strike an awe upon the thousands of Israel, would convince them that the ark was never the less venerable for its having been so long in mean circumstances, and thus he would teach them to rejoice with trembling, and always to treat holy things with reverence and holy fear. 5. God would hereby teach us that a good intention will not justify a bad action; it will not suffice to say of that which is ill done that it was well meant. He will let us know that he can and will secure his ark, and needs not any man's sin to help him to do it. 6. If it was so great a crime for one to lay hold on the ark of the covenant that had no right to do so, what is it for those to lay claim to the privileges of the covenant that come not up to the terms of it? To the wicked God says, <hi type="italic">What hast thou to do to take my covenant in thy mouth?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.16">Ps. l. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Friend, how camest thou in hither?</hi> If the ark was so sacred, and not to be touched irreverently, what is the <hi type="italic">blood of the covenant?</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">Heb. x. 29</reference>. <div eID="gen6059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6060" type="x-p"/> III. David's feelings on the infliction of this stroke were keen, and perhaps not altogether as they should have been. He should have humbled himself under God's hand, confessed his error, acknowledged God's righteousness, and deprecated the further tokens of his displeasure, and then have gone on with the good work he had in hand. But we find, 1. He was displeased. It is not said because Uzzah had affronted God, but because God had made a breach upon Uzzah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">David's anger was kindled.</hi> It is the same word that is used for God's displeasure, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.7">v. 7</reference>. Because God was angry, David was angry and out of humour. As if God might not assert the honour of his ark, and frown upon one that touched it rudely, without asking David leave. Shall mortal man pretend to be more just than God, arraign his proceedings, or charge him with iniquity? David did not now act like himself, like <hi type="italic">a man after God's own heart.</hi> It is not for us to be displeased at any thing that God does, how unpleasing soever it is to us. The death of Uzzah was indeed an eclipse to the glory of a solemnity which David valued himself upon more than any thing else, and might give birth to some speculations among those that were disaffected to him, as if God were departing from him too; but he ought nevertheless to have subscribed to the righteousness and wisdom of God in it, and not to have been displeased at it. When we lie under God's anger we must keep under our own. 2. He was afraid, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.9">v. 9</reference>. It should seem he was afraid with amazement; for he said, <hi type="italic">How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?</hi> As if God sought advantages against all that were about him, and was so extremely tender of his ark that there was no dealing with it; and therefore better for him to keep it at a distance. <hi type="italic">Que procul a Jove, procul a fulmine—To retire from Jove is to retire from the thunder-bolt.</hi> He should rather have said, "Let the ark come to me, and I will take warning by this to treat it with more reverence." <hi type="italic">Provoke me not</hi> (says God, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">and I will do you no hurt.</hi> Or this may be looked upon as a good use which David made of this tremendous judgment. He did not say, "Surely Uzzah was a sinner above all men, because he suffered such things," but is concerned for himself, as one conscious, not only of his own unworthiness of God's favour, but his obnoxiousness to God's displeasure. "God might justly strike me dead as he did Uzzah. <hi type="italic">My flesh trembles for fear of thee,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>. This God intends in his judgments, that others may hear and fear. David therefore will not bring the ark into his own city (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.10">v. 10</reference>) till he is better prepared for its reception. 3. He took care to perpetuate the remembrance of this stroke by a new name he gave to the place: <hi type="italic">Perez-uzzah, the breach of Uzzah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8">v. 8</reference>. He had been lately triumphing in the breach made upon his enemies, and called the place <hi type="italic">Baal-perazim, a place of breaches.</hi> But here is a breach upon his friends. When we see one breach, we should consider that we know not where the next will be. The memorial of this stroke would be a warning to posterity to take heed of all rashness and irreverence in dealing about holy things; for <hi type="italic">God will be sanctified in those that come nigh unto him.</hi> 4. He lodged the ark in a good house, the house of Obed-edom a Levite, which happened to be near the place where this disaster happened, and there, (1.) It was kindly entertained and welcomed, and continued there <hi type="italic">three months,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.10-2Sam.6.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Obed-edom knew what slaughter the ark had made among the Philistines that imprisoned it and the Bethshemites that looked into it. He saw Uzzah struck dead for touching it, and perceived that David himself was afraid of meddling with it; yet he cheerfully invites it to his own house, and opens his doors to it without fear, knowing it was a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death</hi> only to those that treated it ill. "O the courage," says bishop Hall, "of an honest and faithful heart! nothing can make God otherwise than amiable to his own people: even his very justice is lovely." (2.) It paid well for its entertainment: <hi type="italic">The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household.</hi> The same hand that punished Uzzah's proud presumption rewarded Obed-edom's humble boldness, and made the ark to him a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life.</hi> Let none think the worse of the gospel for the judgements inflicted on those that reject it, but set in opposition to them the blessings it brings to those that duly receive it. None ever had, nor ever shall have, reason to say that <hi type="italic">it is in vain to serve God.</hi> Let masters of families be encouraged to keep up religion in their families, and to serve God and the interests of his kingdom with their houses and estates, for that is the way to bring a blessing upon all they have. The ark is a guest which none shall lose by that bid it welcome. Josephus says that, whereas before Obed-edom was poor, on a sudden, in these three months, his estate increased, to the envy of his neighbours. Piety is the best friend to prosperity. In wisdom's left hand are riches and honour. His household shared in the blessing. It is good living in a family that entertains the ark, for all about it will fare the better for it.
entries.31bede014d92b63e0be3fa7d9115b81b027a0f61: <div eID="gen6060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Michal Despises David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen6061" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And it was told king David, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath blessed the house of Obed-edom, and all that <hi type="italic">pertaineth</hi> unto him, because of the ark of God. So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom into the city of David with gladness. <hi type="super">13</hi> And it was <hi type="italic">so,</hi> that when they that bare the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David danced before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with all <hi type="italic">his</hi> might; and David <hi type="italic">was</hi> girded with a linen ephod. <hi type="super">15</hi> So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet. <hi type="super">16</hi> And as the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and she despised him in her heart. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they brought in the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and set it in his place, in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it: and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> And as soon as David had made an end of offering burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he dealt among all the people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> among the whole multitude of Israel, as well to the women as men, to every one a cake of bread, and a good piece <hi type="italic">of flesh,</hi> and a flagon <hi type="italic">of wine.</hi> So all the people departed every one to his house. <div eID="gen6061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6062" type="x-p"/> We have here the second attempt to bring the ark home to the city of David; and this succeeded, though the former miscarried. <div eID="gen6062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6063" type="x-p"/> I. It should seem the blessing with which the house of Obed-edom was blessed for the ark's sake was a great inducement to David to bring it forward; for when that was told him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12">v. 12</reference>) he hastened to fetch it to him. For, 1. It was an evidence that God was reconciled to them, and his anger was turned away. As David could read God's frowns upon them all in Uzzah's stroke, so he could read God's favour to them all in Obed-edom's prosperity; and, if God be at peace with them, they can cheerfully go on with their design. 2. It was an evidence that the ark was not such a burdensome stone as it was taken to be, but, on the contrary, happy was the man that had it near him. Christ is indeed a <hi type="italic">stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence,</hi> to those that are disobedient; but to those who believe he is a <hi type="italic">corner-stone, elect, precious,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6-1Pet.2.8">1 Pet. ii. 6-8</reference>. When David heard that Obed-edom had such joy of the ark, then he would have it in his own city. Note, The experience others have had of the gains of godliness should encourage us to be religious. Is the ark a blessing to others' houses? let us bid it welcome to ours; we may have it, and the blessing of it, without fetching it from our neighbours. <div eID="gen6063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6064" type="x-p"/> II. Let us see how David managed the matter now. 1. He rectified the former error. He did not put the ark in a cart now, but ordered those whose business it was to carry it on their shoulders. This is implied here (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.13">v. 13</reference>) and expressed <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.15">1 Chron. xv. 15</reference>. Then we make a good use of the judgments of God on ourselves and others when we are awakened by them to reform and amend whatever has been amiss. 2. At their first setting out he offered sacrifices to God (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.13">v. 13</reference>) by way of atonement for their former errors and in a thankful acknowledgment of the blessings bestowed on the house of Obed-edom. Then we are likely to speed in our enterprises when we begin with God and give diligence to make our peace with him, When we attend upon God in holy ordinances our eye must be to the great sacrifice, to which we owe it that we are taken into covenant and communion with God, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Ps. l. 5</reference>. 3. He himself attended the solemnity with the highest expressions of joy that could be (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">He danced before the Lord with all his might;</hi> he leaped for joy, as one transported with the occasion, and the more because of the disappointment he met with the last time. It is a pleasure to a good man to see his errors rectified and himself in the way of his duty. His dancing, I suppose, was not artificial, by any certain rule or measure, nor do we find that any danced with him; but it was a natural expression of his great joy and exultation of mind. He did it with all his might; so we should perform all our religious services, as those that are intent upon them and desire to do them in the best manner. All our might is little enough to be employed in holy duties: the work deserves it all. On this occasion David laid aside his imperial purple, and put on a plain linen ephod, which was light and convenient for dancing, and was used in religious exercises by those who were no priests, for Samuel wore one, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.18">1 Sam. ii. 18</reference>. That great prince thought it no disparagement to him to appear in the habit of a minister to the ark. 4. All the people triumphed in this advancement of the ark (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">They brought it up</hi> into the royal city <hi type="italic">with shouting,</hi> and <hi type="italic">with sound of trumpet,</hi> so expressing their own joy in loud acclamations, and giving notice to all about them to rejoice with them. The public and free administration of ordinances, not only under the protection, but under the smiles, of the civil powers, is just matter of rejoicing to any people. 5. the ark was safely brought to, and honourably deposited in, the place prepared for it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17">v. 17</reference>. They set it in <hi type="italic">the midst of the tabernacle,</hi> or tent, <hi type="italic">which David had pitched for it;</hi> not the tabernacle which Moses reared, for that was at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.1.13">2 Chron. i. 13</reference>), and, we may suppose, being made of cloth, in so many hundred years it had gone to decay and was not fit to be removed; but this was a tent set up on purpose to receive the ark. He would not bring it into a private house, no, not his own, lest it should seem to be too much engrossed, and people's resort to it, to pray before it, should be less free; yet he would not build a house for it, lest that should supersede the building of a more stately temple in due time, and therefore, for the present, he placed it within curtains, under a canopy, in imitation of Moses's tabernacle. As soon as ever it was lodged, he offered burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, in thankfulness to God that the business was now done without any more errors or breaches, and in supplication to God for the continuance of his favour. Note, All our joys must be sanctified both with praises and prayers; <hi type="italic">for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.</hi> Now, it should seem, he penned the <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1-Ps.132.8">132nd Psalm</reference>. 6. The people were then dismissed with great satisfaction. He sent them away, (1.) With a gracious prayer: <hi type="italic">He blessed them in the name of the Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.18">v. 18</reference>), having not only a particular interest in heaven as a prophet, but an authority over them as a prince; for <hi type="italic">the less is blessed of the better,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.7">Heb. vii. 7</reference>. He prayed to God to bless them, and particularly to reward them for the honour and respect they had now shown to his ark, assuring them they should be no losers by their journey, but the blessing of God upon their affairs at home would more than bear their charges. He testified his desire for their welfare by this prayer for them, and let them know they had a king that loved them. (2.) With a generous treat; for so it was, rather than a distribution of alms. The great men, it is probable, he entertained at his own house, but to the <hi type="italic">multitude of Israel, men</hi> and <hi type="italic">women</hi> (and <hi type="italic">children,</hi> says Josephus), he dealt to every one a <hi type="italic">cake of bread (a spice-cake,</hi> so some), <hi type="italic">a good piece of flesh—a handsome decent piece</hi> (so some)—<hi type="italic">a part of the peace-offerings</hi> (so Josephus), that they might feast with him <hi type="italic">upon the sacrifice,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">flagon,</hi> or bottle, <hi type="italic">of wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.19">v. 19</reference>. Probably he ordered this provision to be made for them at their respective quarters, and this he did, [1.] In token of his joy and gratitude to God. When the heart is enlarged in cheerfulness the hand should be opened in liberality. The feast of Purim was observed with <hi type="italic">sending portions one to another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">Esth. ix. 22</reference>. As those to whom God is merciful ought to show mercy in forgiving, so those to whom God is bountiful ought to exercise bounty in giving. [2.] To recommend himself to the people, and confirm his interest in them; for <hi type="italic">every one is a friend to him that giveth gifts.</hi> Those that cared not for his prayers would love him for his generosity; and this would encourage them to attend him another time if he saw cause to call them together.
entries.09d0487cb0bb4c873e988109699ef5784756f8f1: <div eID="gen6064" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Expostulates with Michal. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen6065" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself! <hi type="super">21</hi> And David said unto Michal, <hi type="italic">It was</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , over Israel: therefore will I play before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour. <hi type="super">23</hi> Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death. <div eID="gen6065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6066" type="x-p"/> David, having dismissed the congregation with a blessing, <hi type="italic">returned to bless his household</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">v. 20</reference>), that is, to pray with them and for them, and to offer up his family thanksgiving for this national mercy. Ministers must not think that their public performances will excuse them from their family-worship; but when they have, with their instructions and prayers, blessed the solemn assemblies, they must return in the same manner to bless their households, for with them they are in a particular manner charged. David, though he had prophets, and priests, and Levites, about him, to be his chaplains, yet did not devolve the work upon them, but himself <hi type="italic">blessed his household.</hi> It is angels' work to worship God, and therefore surely that can be no disparagement to the greatest of men. <div eID="gen6066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6067" type="x-p"/> Never did David return to his house with so much pleasure and satisfaction as he did now that he had got the ark into his neighbourhood; and yet even this joyful day concluded with some uneasiness, occasioned by the pride and peevishness of his wife. Even the palaces of princes are not exempt from domestic troubles. David had pleased all the multitude of Israel, but Michal was not pleased with his dancing before the ark. For this, when he was at a distance, she scorned him, and when he came home she scolded him. She was not displeased at his generosity to the people, nor did she grudge the entertainment he gave them; but she thought he degraded himself too much in dancing before the ark. It was not her covetousness, but her pride, that made her fret. <div eID="gen6067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6068" type="x-p"/> I. When she saw David in the street dancing before the Lord she <hi type="italic">despised him in her heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.16">v. 16</reference>. She thought this mighty zeal of his for the ark of God, and the transport of joy he was in upon its coming home to him, was but a foolish thing, and unbecoming so great a soldier, and statesman, and monarch, as he was. It would have been enough for him to encourage the devotion of others, but she looked upon it as a thing below him to appear so very devout himself. "What a fool" (thinks she) "does my husband make of himself now! How fond is he of this ark, that might as well have lain still where it had lain for so many years! Much devotion has almost made him mad." Note, The exercises of religion appear very mean in the eyes of those that have little or no religion themselves. <div eID="gen6068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6069" type="x-p"/> II. When he came home in the very best disposition she began to upbraid him, and was so full of disdain and indignation that she could not contain till she had him in private, but went out to meet him with her reproaches. Observe, <div eID="gen6069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6070" type="x-p"/> 1. How she taunted him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">How glorious was the king of Israel to-day!</hi> What a figure didst thou make to-day in the midst of the mob! How unbecoming thy post and character!" Her contempt of him and his devotion began in the heart, but out of the abundance of that the mouth spoke. That which displeased her was his affection to the ark, which she wished he had no greater kindness for than she had: but she basely represents his conduct, in dancing before the ark, as lewd and immodest; and, while really she was displeased at it as a diminution to his honour, she pretended to dislike it as a reproach to his virtue, that he <hi type="italic">uncovered himself in the eyes of the maid-servants,</hi> as no man would have done but <hi type="italic">one of the vain fellows</hi> that cared not how much he shamed himself. We have no reason to think that this was true in fact. David, no doubt, observed decorum, and governed his zeal with discretion. But it is common for those that reproach religion thus to put false colours upon it and lay it under the most odious characters. To have abused any man thus for his pious zeal would have been very profane, but to abuse her own husband thus, whom she ought to have reverenced, and one whose prudence and virtue were above the reach of malice itself to disparage, one who had shown such affection for her that he would not accept a crown unless he might have her restored to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>), was a most base and wicked thing, and showed her to have more of Saul's daughter in her than of David's wife or Jonathan's sister. <div eID="gen6070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6071" type="x-p"/> 2. How he replied to her reproach. He did not upbraid her with her treacherous departure from him to embrace the bosom of a stranger. He had forgiven that, and therefore had forgotten it, though, it may be, his own conscience, on this occasion, upbraided him with his folly in receiving her again (for that is said to pollute the land, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jer. iii. 1</reference>), but he justifies himself in what he did. <div eID="gen6071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6072" type="x-p"/> (1.) He designed thereby to honour God (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">It was before the Lord,</hi> and with an eye to him. Whatever invidious construction she was pleased to put upon it, he had the testimony of his conscience for him that he sincerely aimed at the glory of God, for whom he thought he could never do enough. Here he reminds her indeed of the setting aside of her father's house, to make way for him to the throne, that she might not think herself the most proper judge of propriety: "<hi type="italic">God chose me before thy father, and appointed me to be ruler over Israel,</hi> and now I am the fountain of honour; and, if the expressions of a warm devotion to God were looked upon as mean and unfashionable in thy father's court, yet <hi type="italic">I will play before the Lord,</hi> and thereby bring them into reputation again. And, if this be to be vile (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will be yet more vile.</hi>" Note, [1.] We should be afraid of censuring the devotion of others though it may not agree with our sentiments, because, for aught that we know, the heart may be upright in it, and who are we that we should despise those whom God has accepted? [2.] If we can approve ourselves to God in what we do in religion, and do it as before the Lord, we need not value the censures and reproaches of men. If we appear right in God's eyes, no matter how mean we appear in the eyes of the world. [3.] The more we are vilified for well-doing the more resolute we should be in it, and hold our religion the faster, and bind it the closer to us, for the endeavours of Satan's agents to shake us and to shame us out of it. <hi type="italic">I will be yet more vile.</hi> <div eID="gen6072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6073" type="x-p"/> (2.) He designed thereby to humble himself: "<hi type="italic">I will be base in my own sight,</hi> and will think nothing too mean to stoop to for the honour of God." In the throne of judgment, and in the field of battle, none shall do more to support the grandeur and authority of a prince than David shall; but in acts of devotion he lays aside the thought of majesty, humbles himself to the dust before the Lord, joins in with the meanest services done in honour of the ark, and thinks all this no diminution to him. The greatest of men is less than the least of the ordinances of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen6073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6074" type="x-p"/> (3.) He doubted not but even this would turn to his reputation among those whose reproach Michal pretended to fear: <hi type="italic">Of the maid-servants shall I be had in honour.</hi> The common people would be so far from thinking the worse of him for these pious condescensions that they would esteem and honour him so much the more. Those that are truly pious are sometimes <hi type="italic">manifested in the consciences</hi> even of those that speak ill of them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2 Cor. v. 11</reference>. Let us never be driven from our duty by the fear of reproach; for to be steady and resolute in it will perhaps turn to our reputation more than we think it will. Piety will have its praise. Let us not then be indifferent in it, nor afraid or ashamed to own it. <div eID="gen6074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6075" type="x-p"/> David was contented thus to justify himself, and did not any further animadvert upon Michal's insolence; but God punished her for it, writing her for ever childless from this time forward, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.23">v. 23</reference>. She unjustly reproached David for his devotion, and therefore God justly put her under the perpetual reproach of barrenness. <hi type="italic">Those that honour God he will honour;</hi> but those that despise him, and his servants and service, <hi type="italic">shall be lightly esteemed.</hi>  <chapter eID="2Sam.6"/> <div eID="gen6075" type="x-p"/>

entries.781677ea9bb28e66e950a2fed5ad38d818b0a8b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2868"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen3948" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.5">2Sa 6:1-5</reference>. David Fetches the Ark from Kirjath-jearim on a New Cart.<div eID="gen3948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2868"/><hi type="bold">1. Again, David gathered together all the chosen men of Israel--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>). The object of this second assembly was to commence a national movement for establishing the ark in Jerusalem, after it had continued nearly fifty years in the house of Abinadab (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1">1Ch 13:1</reference>). <div eID="gen3949" type="x-p"/>
entries.f554a84c5b2dc04befcbb37034f3b201d1626338: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2869"/><div sID="gen3950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2869"/><hi type="bold">2. from Baale of Judah--</hi>A very large force of picked men were selected for this important work lest the undertaking might be opposed or obstructed by the Philistines. Besides, a great concourse of people accompanied them out of veneration for the sacred article. The journey to Baale, which is related (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1Ch 13:6</reference>), is here presupposed, and the historian describes the course of the procession from that place to the capital. <div eID="gen3950" type="x-p"/>
entries.1801d9f824ff17c3cab4e1834efdc8a2478b19d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2870"/><div sID="gen3951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2870"/><hi type="bold">3. they set the ark of God upon a new cart--</hi>or a covered wagon (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.7">1Sa 6:7</reference>). This was a hasty and inconsiderate procedure, in violation of an express statute (see on <reference osisRef="Num.4.15">Nu 4:15</reference> and see <reference osisRef="Num.7.9">Nu 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.18.3">18:3</reference>).<div eID="gen3951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3952" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6-2Sam.6.11">2Sa 6:6-11</reference>. Uzzah Smitten. <div eID="gen3952" type="x-p"/>
entries.49f981bfa68336eb463f1480b6faecd877f0f61e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2871"/><div sID="gen3953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2871"/><hi type="bold">6-8. they came to Nachon's threshing-floor--</hi>or Chidon's (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.9">1Ch 13:9</reference>). The Chaldee version renders the words, "came to the place prepared for the reception of the ark," that is, near the city of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.13">2Sa 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen3953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the oxen shook it--</hi>or, "stumbled" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.9">1Ch 13:9</reference>). Fearing that the ark was in danger of being overturned, Uzzah, under the impulse of momentary feeling, laid hold of it to keep it steady. Whether it fell and crushed him, or some sudden disease attacked him, he fell dead upon the spot. This melancholy occurrence not only threw a cloud over the joyous scene, but entirely stopped the procession; for the ark was left where it then was, in the near neighborhood of the capital. It is of importance to observe the proportionate severity of the punishments attending the profanation of the ark. The Philistines suffered by diseases, from which they were relieved by their oblations, because the law had not been given to them [1Sa 5:8-12]; the Bethshemites also suffered, but not fatally [1Sa 6:19]; their error proceeded from ignorance or inadvertency. But Uzzah, who was a Levite, and well instructed, suffered death for his breach of the law. The severity of Uzzah's fate may seem to us too great for the nature and degree of the offense. But it does not become us to sit in judgment on the dispensations of God; and, besides, it is apparent that the divine purpose was to inspire awe of His majesty, a submission to His law, and a profound veneration for the symbols and ordinances of His worship. <div eID="gen3954" type="x-p"/>
entries.955e18372979632a79c937ff7cfc519dadce4181: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2872"/><div sID="gen3955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2872"/><hi type="bold">9-10. David was afraid of the Lord that day, &c.--</hi>His feelings on this alarming judgment were greatly excited on various accounts, dreading that the displeasure of God had been provoked by the removal of the ark, that the punishment would be extended to himself and people, and that they might fall into some error or neglect during the further conveyance of the ark. He resolved, therefore, to wait for more light and direction as to the path of duty. An earlier consultation by Urim would have led him right at the first, whereas in this perplexity and distress, he was reaping the fruits of inconsideration and neglect. <div eID="gen3955" type="x-p"/>
entries.2009ee92b449d2c058253486aee26c4d69821382: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2873"/><div sID="gen3956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2873"/><hi type="bold">11. Obed-edom the Gittite--</hi>a Levite (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.24">21, 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.4">26:4</reference>). He is called a Gittite, either from his residence at Gath, or more probably from Gath-rimmon, one of the Levitical cities (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.24">Jos 21:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.21.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen3956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3957" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.19">2Sa 6:12-19</reference>. David Afterwards Brings the Ark to Zion. <div eID="gen3957" type="x-p"/>
entries.638eda20b077094555097c5a43fa3d8104315557: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2874"/><div sID="gen3958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2874"/><hi type="bold">12. it was told king David, saying, The Lord hath blessed the house of Obed-edom, and all that pertaineth unto him, because of the ark of God--</hi>The lapse of three months not only restored the agitated mind of the monarch to a tranquil and settled tone, but led him to a discovery of his former error. Having learned that the ark was kept in its temporary resting-place not only without inconvenience or danger, but with great advantage, he resolved forthwith to remove it to the capital, with the observance of all due form and solemnity (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.1-1Chr.15.13">1Ch 15:1-13</reference>). It was transported now on the shoulders of the priests, who had been carefully prepared for the work, and the procession was distinguished by extraordinary solemnities and demonstrations of joy. <div eID="gen3958" type="x-p"/>
entries.0990edd102f39de85c3064d2dba7ac19e1caef09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2875"/><div sID="gen3959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2875"/><hi type="bold">13. when they that bare the ark ... had gone six paces--</hi>Some think that four altars were hastily raised for the offering of sacrifices at the distance of every six paces (but see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.26">1Ch 15:26</reference>). <div eID="gen3959" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca407a5fd061d11c9d7ff9909eb1251ccd409812: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2876"/><div sID="gen3960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2876"/><hi type="bold">14. David danced before the Lord--</hi>The Hebrews, like other ancient people, had their sacred dances, which were performed on their solemn anniversaries and other great occasions of commemorating some special token of the divine goodness and favor.<div eID="gen3960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with all his might--</hi>intimating violent efforts of leaping, and divested of his royal mantle (in a state of undress), conduct apparently unsuitable to the gravity of age or the dignity of a king. But it was unquestionably done as an act of religious homage, his attitudes and dress being symbolic, as they have always been in Oriental countries, of penitence, joy, thankfulness, and devotion. [See on <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference>.] <div eID="gen3961" type="x-p"/>
entries.60810ce3d3ef7eba6d890d1a6941f258923d82d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2877"/><div sID="gen3962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2877"/><hi type="bold">17. they brought in the ark of the Lord, and set it in his place, in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it--</hi>The old tabernacle remained at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.29">21:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>). Probably it was not removed because it was too large for the temporary place the king had appropriated, and because he contemplated the building of a temple. <div eID="gen3962" type="x-p"/>
entries.d79a5c58af6a40cc6356409538b2a9ccb96fb408: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2878"/><div sID="gen3963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2878"/><hi type="bold">18. he blessed the people--</hi>in the double character of prophet and king (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.55">1Ki 8:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.56">56</reference>). [See on <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.2">1Ch 16:2</reference>.] <div eID="gen3963" type="x-p"/>
entries.6346efe0036abec7377b0b66d67d8a4ca6615798: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2879"/><div sID="gen3964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2879"/><hi type="bold">19. cake of bread--</hi>unleavened and slender.<div eID="gen3964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a good piece of flesh--</hi>roast beef.<div eID="gen3965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3966" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20-2Sam.6.23">2Sa 6:20-23</reference>. Michal's Barrenness. <div eID="gen3966" type="x-p"/>
entries.19a55c0d782ec1f9a0c313017a62659e7ff3c094: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2880"/><div sID="gen3967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2880"/><hi type="bold">20-22. Michal ... came out to meet David, &c.--</hi>Proud of her royal extraction, she upbraided her husband for lowering the dignity of the crown and acting more like a buffoon than a king. But her taunting sarcasm was repelled in a manner that could not be agreeable to her feelings while it indicated the warm piety and gratitude of David. <chapter eID="2Sam.6"/>

entries.d9b03e860ba9087343d78951bf3b15a74421f7ce: <div eID="gen10821" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10822" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10823" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10823" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10822" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10824" type="x-p"/> David goes with thirty thousand men to being the ark from Kiriath-jearim to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.5">2Sam 6:1-5</reference>. The ox stumbling, Uzzah, who drove the cart on which the ark was placed, put forth his hand to save it from falling: the Lord was displeased, and smote him so that he died, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6">2Sam 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.7">2Sam 6:7</reference>. David, being alarmed, carries the ark to the house of Obed-edom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8-2Sam.6.10">2Sam 6:8-10</reference>. Here it remained three months; and God prospered Obed-edom, in whose house it was deposited, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.11">2Sam 6:11</reference>. David, hearing of this, brings the ark, with sacrifices and solemn rejoicings, to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12-2Sam.6.15">2Sam 6:12-15</reference>. Michal, seeing David dance before the ark, despises him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.16">2Sam 6:16</reference>. He offers burnt-offerings and peace offerings, and deals among all the people, men and women, a cake of bread, a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine each, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17-2Sam.6.19">2Sam 6:17-19</reference>. Michal coming to meet him, and seeing him dance extravagantly before the ark, reproaches him for his conduct: he vindicates himself, reproves her, and she dies childless, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20-2Sam.6.23">2Sam 6:20-23</reference>. <div eID="gen10824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10825" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10826" type="x-p"/> Thirty thousand - This is supposed to have been a new levy; and thus he augmented his army by 30,000 fresh troops. The Septuagint has 70,000.
entries.d6b2c7f21db484de198abd8a5247e5e3ac8f288b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10827" type="x-p"/> From Baale of Judah - This is supposed to be the same city which, in <reference osisRef="Jos.15.60">Jos 15:60</reference>, is called Kirjah-baal or Kirjath-jearim; (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1Chr 13:6</reference>); or Baalah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.9">Jos 15:9</reference>. <div eID="gen10827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10828" type="x-p"/> Whose name is called by the name of the Lord - That is, The ark is called the ark of the Lord of hosts. But this is not a literal version; the word שם shem, Name, occurs twice together; probably one of them should be read שם sham, There. There the name of the Lord of hosts was invoked, etc.
entries.5bcf47200d311a8525ea7f5db0b7c5ad1e7b9b35: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10829" type="x-p"/> A new cart - Every thing used in the worship of God was hallowed or set apart for that purpose: a new cart was used through respect, as that had never been applied to any profane or common purpose. But this was not sufficient, for the ark should have been carried on the shoulders of the priests; and the neglect of this ceremony was the cause of the death of Uzzah.
entries.8a7e8bcafe18433bf0b2a86f33dce3b9c227558f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10830" type="x-p"/> On all manner of instruments made of fir wood - This place should be corrected from the parallel place, <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.8">1Chr 13:8</reference> : "All Israel played before God, with all their might, and with singing, and with harps, and with psalteries," etc. Instead of בכל עצי bechol atsey, "with all woods" or "trees;" the parallel place is בכל עז bechol oz. "with all their strength:" this makes a good sense, the first makes none. The Septuagint, in this place, has the verse reading; εν ισχυΐ, with might.
entries.861f8143c7f9efab9311e1dd698779a1d0bfcb77: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10831" type="x-p"/> Uzzah put forth his hand - In <reference osisRef="Num.4.15-Num.4.20">Num 4:15-20</reference>, the Levites are forbidden to touch the ark on pain of death, this penalty was inflicted upon Uzzah, and he was the first that suffered for a breach of this law.
entries.713c9e9e92f1a50ab0ebc2d0d3904d7a32155e98: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10832" type="x-p"/> Smote him there for his error - Uzzah sinned through ignorance and precipitancy; he had not time to reflect, the oxen suddenly stumbled; and, fearing lest the ark should fall, he suddenly stretched out his hand to prevent it. Had he touched the ark with impunity, the populace might have lost their respect for it and its sacred service, the example of Uzzah must have filled them with fear and sacred reverence; and, as to Uzzah, no man can doubt of his eternal safety. He committed a sin unto death, but doubtless the mercy of God was extended to his soul.
entries.2df263d1e6d1bbb47baea5df1a415affe278b8ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10833" type="x-p"/> But David carried it aside - The house of Obed-edom appears to have been very near the city, which they were about to enter, but were prevented by this accident, and lodged the ark with the nearest friend.
entries.b02cef10b6a7020bb29092a8282520a5165e432e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10834" type="x-p"/> The Lord blessed Obed-edom - And why? Because he had the ark of the Lord in his house. Whoever entertains God's messengers, or consecrates his house to the service of God, will infallibly receive God's blessing.
entries.8a0a26733b3590ed0df9377547379a02aa2667fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10835" type="x-p"/> So David - brought up the ark - The Vulgate adds to this verse: And David had seven choirs, and a calf for a sacrifice. The Septuagint make a greater addition: "And he had seven choirs carrying the ark, a sacrifice, a calf, and lambs. And David played on harmonious organs before the Lord; and David was clothed with a costly tunic; and David and all the house of Israel, brought the ark of the Lord with rejoicing, and the sound of a trumpet." Nothing of this is found in any MS., nor in the Chaldee, the Syriac, nor the Arabic, nor in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.25">1Chr 15:25</reference>.
entries.2e38bcb66135e277658eb3edefcfcb26308d1e32: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10836" type="x-p"/> And David danced before the Lord - Dancing is a religious ceremony among the Hindoos, and they consider it an act of devotion to their idols. It is evident that David considered it in the same light. What connection dancing can have with devotion I cannot tell. This I know, that unpremeditated and involuntary skipping may be the effect of sudden mental elation.
entries.a745cf2b391e03d3c408083182f7bb530bdba078: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10837" type="x-p"/> She despised him in her heart - She did not blame him outwardly; she thought he had disgraced himself, but she kept her mind to herself.
entries.3e17751620581865b774182aa56c4bed4dc75984: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10838" type="x-p"/> He blessed the people in the name of the Lord - David acted here as priest, for it was the general prerogative of the priests to bless the people, but it appears, by both David and Solomon, that it was the prerogative of the kings also.
entries.fa288e5b2c8c58481184c2ed65da147acb0e782c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10839" type="x-p"/> A cake of bread - Such as those which are baked without leaven, and are made very thin. <div eID="gen10839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10840" type="x-p"/> A good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine - The words of flesh and of wine we add; they are not in the Hebrew. The Chaldee translates one part and one portion; but all the other versions understand the Hebrew as we do.
entries.e818bf5d1bc74d5eb12fb13736d9ab7b3c9058b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10841" type="x-p"/> To bless his household - This was according to the custom of the patriarchs, who were priests in their own families. It is worthy of remark, that David is called patriarch by Stephen, <reference osisRef="Act.2.29">Act 2:29</reference>, though living upwards of four hundred years after the termination of the patriarchal age. <div eID="gen10841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10842" type="x-p"/> How glorious was the king of Israel - This is a strong irony. From what Michal says, it is probable that David used some violent gesticulations, by means of which some parts of his body became uncovered. But it is very probable that we cannot guess all that was implied in this reproach.
entries.b311fc4fcc04b981ab203e2e38784562d8d4ef5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10843" type="x-p"/> It was before the Lord, which chose me - David felt the reproach, and was strongly irritated, and seems to have spoken to Michal with sufficient asperity.
entries.b7b0dc21e331c2a7bea5a14eedd7cfd1d99bb693: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10844" type="x-p"/> I will yet be more vile - The plain meaning of these words appears to be this: "I am not ashamed of humbling myself before that God who rejected thy father because of his obstinacy and pride, and chose me in his stead to rule his people; and even those maid-servants, when they come to know the motive of my conduct, shall acknowledge its propriety, and treat me with additional respect; and as for thee, thou shalt find that thy conduct is as little pleasing to God as it is to me." Then it is said, Michal had no child till the day of her death: probably David never more took her to his bed; or God, in his providence, might have subjected her to barrenness which in Palestine was considered both a misfortune and a reproach. Michal formed her judgment without reason, and meddled with that which she did not understand. We should be careful how we attribute actions, the reasons of which we cannot comprehend, to motives which may appear to us unjustifiable or absurd. Rash judgments are doubly pernicious; they hurt those who form them, and those of whom they are formed.  <chapter eID="2Sam.6"/> <div eID="gen10844" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e35668a3f55fe076bad26dc8d8a42184ef33fd5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1">2Sa 6:1</reference> <hi type="italic">The ark fetched from Kirjath-jearim.</hi> - 2Sa 6:1. <hi type="italic">“David assembled together again all the chosen men in Israel, thirty thousand.”</hi> יסף for יאסף is the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of אסף, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sa 15:6</reference>; Psa 104:29. עוד, <hi type="italic">again, once more,</hi> points back to <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:3</reference>, where all Israel is said to have assembled for the first time in Hebron to anoint David king. It is true that that assembly was not convened directly by David himself; but this was not the point in question, but merely their assembling a second time (see Bertheau on <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1Ch 13:5</reference>). בּחוּר does not mean “the young men” here (νεάνια, lxx), or “the fighting men,” but, according to the etymology of the word, “the picked men.” Instead of thirty thousand, the lxx have seventy chiliads, probably with an intentional exaggeration, because the number of men in Israel who were capable of bearing arms amounted to more than thirty thousand. The whole nation, through a very considerable body of representatives, was to take part in the removal of the ark. The writer of the Chronicles gives a more elaborate account of the preparations for these festivities (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1-1Chr.13.5">1Ch 13:1-5</reference>); namely, that David took counsel with the heads of thousands and hundreds, and all the leaders, i.e., all the heads of families and households, and then with their consent collected together the whole nation from the brook of Egypt to Hamath, of course not every individual, but a large number of heads of households as representatives of the whole. This account in the Chronicles is not an expansion of the brief notice given here; but the account before us is a condensation of the fuller description given in the sources that were employed by both authors.
entries.51034b5be251f53f1a2a91593fb946c3b78dae27: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2">2Sa 6:2</reference> <hi type="italic">“David went with all the people that were with him to Baale-Jehuda, to fetch up the ark of God from thence.”</hi> The words והוּדה מבּעליcause some difficulty on account of the מן, which is used instead of the accusative with ה <hi type="italic">loc</hi>., like בּעלתה in the Chronicles; yet the translators of the Septuagint, Chaldee, Vulgate, and other versions, all had the reading מן in their text, and בּעלי has therefore been taken as an appellative and rendered ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρχότων Ἰουδά (“from the rulers of Judah”), or as Luther renders it, “from the citizens of Judah.” This is decidedly incorrect, as the word “thence” which follows is perfectly unintelligible on any other supposition than that <hi type="italic">Baale-Jehudah</hi> is the name of a place. <hi type="italic">Baale-Jehudah</hi> is another name of the city of <hi type="italic">Kirjath-jearim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.60">Jos 15:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.14">Jos 18:14</reference>), which is called Baalah in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.9">Jos 15:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1Ch 13:6</reference>, according to its Canaanitish name, instead of which the name <hi type="italic">Kirjath-jearim </hi>(city of the woods) was adopted by the Israelites, though without entirely supplanting the old name. The epithet “of Judah” is a contraction of the fuller expression “city of the children of Judah” in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.14">Jos 18:14</reference>, and is added to distinguish this Baal city, which was situated upon the border of the tribe of Judah, from other cities that were also named after Baal, such as <hi type="italic">Baal</hi> or <hi type="italic">Baalath-beer</hi> in the tribe of Simeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.33">1Ch 4:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.8">Jos 19:8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Baalath</hi> in the tribe of Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.44">Jos 19:44</reference>), the present <hi type="italic">Kuryet el Enab</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>). The מן (from) is either a very ancient error of the pen that crept by accident into the text, or, if genuine and original, it is to be explained on the supposition that the historian dropped the construction with which he started, and instead of mentioning <hi type="italic">Baale-Jehudah</hi> as the place to which David went, gave it at once as the place from which he fetched the ark; so that the passage is to be understood in this way: “And David went, and all the people who were with him, out of Baale-Jehudah, to which they had gone up to fetch the ark of God” (Kimchi). In the sentence which follows, a difficulty is also occasioned by the repetition of the word שׁם in the clause עליו ... נקרא עשׁר, <hi type="italic">“upon which the name is called, the name of Jehovah of hosts, who is enthroned above the cherubim.”</hi> The difficulty cannot be solved by altering the first שׁם into שׁם, as Clericus, Thenius, and Bertheau suggest: for if this alteration were adopted, we should have to render the passage “where the name of Jehovah of hosts is invoked, who is enthroned above the cherubim (which are) upon it (i.e., upon the ark);” and this would not only introduce an unscriptural thought into the passage, but it would be impossible to find any suitable meaning for the word עליו, except by making very arbitrary interpolations. Throughout the whole of the Old Testament we never meet with the idea that the name of Jehovah was invoked at the ark of the covenant, because no one was allowed to approach the ark for the purpose of invoking the name of the Lord there; and upon the great day of atonement the high priest was only allowed to enter the most holy place with the cloud of incense, to sprinkle the blood of the atoning sacrifice upon the ark. Moreover, the standing expression for “call upon the name of the Lord” is יי בשׁם קרא; whereas פּ על יי שׁם נקרא signifies “the name of Jehovah is called above a person or thing.” Lastly, even if עליו belonged to הכּרבים ישׁב, it would not only be a superfluous addition, occurring nowhere else in connection with הך ישׁב, not even in <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1Ch 13:6</reference> (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.4">1Sa 4:4</reference>; 2Ki 19:15; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.16">Isa 37:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1">Psa 99:1</reference>), but such an addition if made at all would necessarily require עליו אשׁר ע (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>). The only way in which we can obtain a biblical thought and grammatical sense is by connecting עליו with the אשׁר before נקרא: “above which (ark) the name of Jehovah-Zebaoth is named,” i.e., above which Jehovah reveals His glory or His divine nature to His people, or manifests His gracious presence in Israel. “The name of God denotes all the operations of God through which He attests His personal presence in that relation into which He has entered to man, i.e., the whole of the divine self-manifestation, or of that side of the divine nature which is turned towards men” (Oehler, Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Encycl.</hi> x. p. 197). From this deeper meaning of “the name of God” we may probably explain the repetition of the word שׁם, which is first of all written absolutely (as at the close of <reference osisRef="Lev.24.16">Lev 24:16</reference>), and then more fully defined as “the name of the Lord of hosts.”
entries.d218cb2d71e2d0a30a594e496824de2ba389f21e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3-2Sam.6.4">2Sa 6:3-4</reference> <hi type="italic">“They set the ark of God upon a new cart, and took it away from the house of Abinadab.”</hi> הרכּיב means here “to put (load) upon a cart,” and נשׂא dn to take away, i.e., drive off: for there are grammatical (or syntactical) reasons which make it impossible to render וישּׂאהוּ as a pluperfect (“they had taken”), on account of the previous וירכבו. <div eID="gen4306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4307" type="x-p"/> The ark of the covenant had been standing in the house of Abinadab from the time when the Philistines had sent it back into the land of Israel, i.e., about seventy years (viz., twenty years to the victory at Ebenezer mentioned in 1Sa 7:1., forty years under Samuel and Saul, and about ten years under David: see the chronological table). The further statement, that “Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, drove the cart,” may easily be reconciled with this. These two sons were either born about the time when the ark was first taken to Abinadab’s house, or at a subsequent period; or else the term sons is used, as is frequently the case, in the sense of grandsons. The words from חדשׁה (the last word in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3">2Sa 6:3</reference>) to <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi> in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.4">2Sa 6:4</reference> are wanting in the Septuagint, and can only have been introduced through the error of a copyist, whose eye wandered back to the first עגלה in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3">2Sa 6:3</reference>, so that he copied a whole line twice over; for they not only contain a pure tautology, a merely verbal and altogether superfluous and purposeless repetition, but they are altogether unsuitable to the connection in which they stand. Not only is there something very strange in the repetition of the חדשׁה without an article after העגלה; but the words which follow, ארון ה עם (with the ark of God), cannot be made to fit on to the repeated clause, for there is no sense whatever in such a sentence as this: “They brought it (the ark) out of the house of Abinadab, which is upon the hill, <hi type="italic">with the</hi> ark of God.” The only way in which the words “with the ark” can be made to acquire any meaning at all, is by omitting the repetition referred to, and connecting them with the new cart in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.3">2Sa 6:3</reference> : “Uzzah and Ahio ... drove the cart with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark.” נהג, to drive (a carriage), is construed here with an accusative, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.7">1Ch 13:7</reference> with בּ, as in Isa 11:6.
entries.2b2b19cdd2dec7aca41ab555a16a8d82a0855c9b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.5">2Sa 6:5</reference> <div eID="gen4307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4308" type="x-p"/> And David and all the house (people) of Israel were משׂחקים, sporting, i.e., they danced and played, before Jehovah. ברושׁים עצי בּכל, “with all kinds of woods of cypresses.” This could only mean, with all kinds of instruments made of cypress wood; but this mode of expression would be a very strange one even if the reading were correct. In the Chronicles, however (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8">2Sa 6:8</reference>), instead of this strange expression, we find וּבשׁירים בּכל־עז, “with all their might and with songs.” This is evidently the correct reading, from which our text has sprung, although the latter is found in all the old versions, and even in the Septuagint, which really combines the two readings thus: ἐν ὀργάνοις ἡρμοσμένοις ἐν ισχύΐ καὶ ἐν ᾠδαῖς, where ἐν ὀργάνοις ἡρμοσμένοις is evidently the interpretation of ברושׁים עצי בּכל; for the text of the Chronicles cannot be regarded as an explanation of Samuel. Moreover, songs would not be omitted on such a festive occasion; and two of the instruments mentioned, viz., the <hi type="italic">kinnor</hi> and <hi type="italic">nebel</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>), were generally played as accompaniments to singing. The <hi type="italic">vav</hi> before בּשׁירים, and before the different instruments, corresponds to the Latin <hi type="italic">et ... et</hi>, both ... and. תּף, the timbrel. וּבצלצלים בּמנענעים, <hi type="italic">sistris et cymbalis</hi> (Vulg., Syr.), “with bells and cymbals” (Luther). מנענעים, from נוּע, are instruments that are shaken, the σεῖστρα, <hi type="italic">sistra</hi>, of the ancients, which consisted of two iron rods fastened together at one end, either in a semicircle or at right angels, upon which rings were hung loosely, so as to make a tinkling sound when they were shaken. צלצלים = מצלתּים are cymbals or castanets. Instead of מנענעים, we find חצצרות, trumpets, mentioned in the Chronicles in the last rank after the cymbals. It is possible that sistra were played and trumpets blown, so that the two accounts complete each other.
entries.288bfceba84690bf9cb6339bf66727d777dc4179: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6-2Sam.6.7">2Sa 6:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen4308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4309" type="x-p"/> When the procession had reached the threshing-floor of <hi type="italic">Nachon</hi>, Uzzah stretched out his hand to lay hold of the ark, i.e., to keep it from falling over with the cart, because the oxen slipped. And the wrath of the Lord was kindled, and God slew Uzzah upon the spot. <hi type="italic">Goren</hi> <hi type="italic">nachon</hi> means “the threshing-floor of the stroke” (<hi type="italic">nachon</hi> from נכה, not from כּוּן); in the Chronicles we have <hi type="italic">goren</hi> <hi type="italic">chidon</hi>, i.e., the threshing-floor of destruction or disaster (כּידון = כּיד, <reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference>). Chidon is probably only an explanation of nachon, so that the name may have been given to the threshing-floor, not from its owner, but from the incident connected with the ark which took place there. Eventually, however, this name was supplanted by the name <hi type="italic">Perez-uzzah</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8">2Sa 6:8</reference>).
