The situation of the threshing-floor cannot be determined, as all that we can gather from this account is that the house of Obed-edom the Gathite was somewhere near it; but no village, hamlet, or town is mentioned.<note placement="foot">If it were possible to discover the situation of Gath-rimmon, the home of Obed-edom (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.10">2Sa 6:10</reference>), we might probably decide the question whether Obed-edom was still living in the town where he was born or not. But according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>., Kirjath-jearim was ten miles from Jerusalem, and Gath-rimmon twelve, that is to say, farther off. Now, if these statements are correct, Obed-edom’s house cannot have been in Gath-rimmon.</note><hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> paraphrases הבּקר שׁמטוּ כּי thus: “Because the oxen kicked and turned it (the ark over.” But שׁמט does not mean to kick; its true meaning is to let go, or let lie (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.2-Deut.15.3">Deu 15:2-3</reference>), hence to slip or stumble. The stumbling of the animals might easily have turned the cart over, and this was what Uzzah tried to prevent by laying hold of the ark. God smote him there “on account of the offence” (שׁל, ἁπ. λεγ. from שׁלה, in the sense of erring, or committing a fault). The writer of the Chronicles gives it thus: “Because he had stretched out his hand to the ark,” though of course the text before us is not to be altered to this, as Thenius and Bertheau suggest.
entries.965194f69244f64e0a158849650e2c522b2719c4: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.8">2Sa 6:8</reference> “And David was angry, because Jehovah had made a rent on Uzzah, and called the place <hi type="italic">Perez-uzzah</hi>” (rent of Uzzah). פּרץ פּרץ, to tear a rent, is here applied to a sudden tearing away from life. ל יחר is understood by many in the sense of “he troubled himself;” but this meaning cannot be grammatically sustained, whilst it is quite possible to become angry, or fall into a state of violent excitement, at an unexpected calamity. The burning of David’s anger was not directed against God, but referred to the calamity which had befallen Uzzah, or speaking more correctly, to the cause of this calamity, which David attributed to himself or to his undertaking. As he had not only resolved upon the removal of the ark, but had also planned the way in which it should be taken to Jerusalem, he could not trace the occasion of Uzzah’s death to any other cause than his own plans. He was therefore angry that such misfortune had attended his undertaking. In his first excitement and dismay, David may not have perceived the real and deeper ground of this divine judgment. Uzzah’s offence consisted in the fact that he had touched the ark with profane feelings, although with good intentions, namely to prevent its rolling over and falling from the cart. Touching the ark, the throne of the divine glory and visible pledge of the invisible presence of the Lord, was a violation of the majesty of the holy God. “Uzzah was therefore a type of all who with good intentions, humanly speaking, yet with unsanctified minds, interfere in the affairs of the kingdom of God, from the notion that they are in danger, and with the hope of saving them” (<hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>). On further reflection, David could not fail to discover where the cause of Uzzah’s offence, which he had atoned for with his life, really had lain, and that it had actually arisen from the fact that he (David) and those about him had decided to disregard the distinct instructions of the law with regard to the handling of the ark. According to Num 4 the ark was not only to be moved by none but Levites, but it was to be carried on the shoulders, not in a carriage; and in Num 4:15, even the Levites were expressly forbidden to touch it on pain of death. But instead of taking these instructions as their rule, they had followed the example of the Philistines when they sent back the ark (1Sa 6:7.), and had placed it upon a new cart, and directed Uzzah to drive it, whilst, as his conduct on the occasion clearly shows, he had no idea of the unapproachable holiness of the ark of God, and had to expiate his offence with his life, as a warning to all the Israelites.
entries.6e7fe2b76bc76331535040cba52d548fdacc060f: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.9-2Sam.6.10">2Sa 6:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4310" type="x-p"/> David’s excitement at what had occurred was soon changed into fear of the Lord, so that he said, “How shall the ark of Jehovah come to me?” If merely touching the ark of God is punished in this way, how can I have it brought near me, up to the citadel of Zion? He therefore relinquished his intention of bringing it into the city of David, and placed it in the house of Obed-edom the Gathite. <hi type="italic">Obed-edom</hi> was a Levite of the family of the Korahites, who sprang from Kohath (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.6.21">Exo 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.18.16">Exo 18:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.4">1Ch 26:4</reference>), and belonged to the class of Levitical doorkeepers, whose duty it was, in connection with other Levites, to watch over the ark in the sacred tent (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:24</reference>). He is called the <hi type="italic">Gittite</hi> or <hi type="italic">Gathite</hi> from his birthplace, the Levitical city of <hi type="italic">Gath-rimmon</hi> in the tribe of Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.24">Jos 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.45">Jos 19:45</reference>).
entries.76b014fb7d7c6fc95bd2ec20393b1bacbf999734: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.11-2Sam.6.12">2Sa 6:11-12</reference> <hi type="italic">Removal of the ark of God to the city of David</hi> (cf. 1 Chron 15). - <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.11">2Sa 6:11</reference>, 2Sa 6:12. When the ark had been in the house of Obed-edom for three months, and David heard that the Lord had blessed his house for the sake of the ark of God, he went thither and brought it up to the city of David with gladness i.e., with festal rejoicing, or a solemn procession. (For שׂמהה, in the sense of festal rejoicing, or a joyous fête, see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.27">Gen 31:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.43">Neh 12:43</reference>, etc.) On this occasion, however, David adhered strictly to the instructions of the law, as the more elaborate account given in the Chronicles clearly shows. He not only gathered together all Israel at Jerusalem to join in this solemn act, but summoned the priests and Levites, and commanded them to sanctify themselves, and carry the ark “according to the right,” i.e., as the Lord had commanded in the law of Moses, and to offer sacrifices during the procession, and sin songs, i.e., psalms, with musical accompaniment. In the very condensed account before us, all that is mentioned is the carrying of the ark, the sacrificing during the march, and the festivities of the king and people. But even from these few facts we see that David had discovered his former mistake, and had given up the idea of removing the ark upon a carriage as a transgression of the law.
entries.c058c677902e6355c7c64037b89c946a4d3520dd: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.13">2Sa 6:13</reference> <div eID="gen4310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4311" type="x-p"/> The bearers of the ark are not particularly mentioned in this account; but it is very evident that they were Levites, as the Chronicles affirm, from the fact that the ark was carried this time, and not driven, as before. <hi type="italic">“And it came to pass, when the bearers of the ark of Jehovah had gone six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fatted calf”</hi> (i.e., had them sacrificed). These words are generally understood as meaning, that sacrifices of this kind were offered along the whole way, at the distance of six paces apart. This would certainly have been a possible thing, and there would be no necessity to assume that the procession halted every six paces, until the sacrificial ceremony was completed, but the ark might have continued in progress, whilst sacrifices were being offered at the distances mentioned. And even the immense number of sacrificial animals that would have been required is no valid objection to such an assumption. We do not know what the distance really was: all that we know is, that it was not so much as ten miles, as Kirjath-jearim was only about twelve miles from Jerusalem, so that a few thousand oxen, and the same number of fatted calves, would have been quite sufficient. But the words of the text do not distinctly affirm that sacrifices were offered whenever the bearers advanced six paces, but only that this was done was soon as the bearers had taken the first six steps. So that, strictly speaking, all that is stated is, that when the procession had started and gone six paces, the sacrifice was offered, namely, for the purpose of inaugurating or consecrating the solemn procession. In 1 Chron 15 this fact is omitted; and it is stated instead (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.26">1Ch 15:26</reference>), that “when God helped the Levites that bare the ark of the covenant of the Lord, they offered seven bullocks and seven rams,” i.e., at the close of the procession, when the journey was ended, to praise God for the fact that the Levites had been enabled to carry the ark of God to the place appointed for it, without suffering the slightest harm.<note placement="foot">There is no discrepancy, therefore, between the two different accounts; but the one supplements the other in a manner perfectly in harmony with the whole affair, - at the outset, a sacrifice consisting of one ox and one fatted calf; and at the close, one of seven oxen and seven rams. Consequently there is no reason for altering the text of the verse before us, as Thenius proposes, according to the senseless rendering of the lxx, καὶ ἦσαν μετ ̓ αὐτοῦ αἴροντες τὴν κιβωτὸν ἑπτὰ χοροί, καὶ θῦμα μόσχος καὶ ἄρνες (“with David there were bearers of the ark, seven choirs, and sacrifices of a calf and lambs”), which has also found its way into the Vulgate, though <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> has rendered our Hebrew text faithfully afterwards (i.e., after the gloss, which was probably taken from the Itala, and inserted in his translation).</note>
entries.8da1ee0261461e94627f5454ac089429732638ed: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.14-2Sam.6.15">2Sa 6:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen4311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4312" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And David danced with all his might before the Lord</hi> (i.e., before the ark), <hi type="italic">and was girded with a white ephod</hi> (shoulder-dress).” Dancing, as an expression of holy enthusiasm, was a customary thing from time immemorial: we meet with it as early as at the festival of thanksgiving at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>); but there, and also at subsequent celebrations of the different victories gained by the Israelites, none but women are described as taking part in it (Jdg 11:34; Jdg 21:19; <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference>). The white ephod was, strictly speaking, a priestly costume, although in the law it is not prescribed as the dress to be worn by them when performing their official duties, but rather as the dress which denoted the priestly character of the wearer (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.18">1Sa 22:18</reference>); and for this reason it was worn by David in connection with these festivities in honour of the Lord, as the head of the priestly nation of Israel (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.18">1Sa 2:18</reference>). In <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.15">2Sa 6:15</reference> it is still further related, that David and all the house (nation) of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord with jubilee and trumpet-blast. תּרוּעה is used here to signify the song of jubilee and the joyous shouting of the people. In the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.28">1Ch 15:28</reference>) the musical instruments played on the occasion are also severally mentioned.
entries.913a0f3e20830744f1f86e81a2d5935c37a53dcd: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.16">2Sa 6:16</reference> <div eID="gen4312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4313" type="x-p"/> When the ark came (i.e., was carried) into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window, and there she saw king David leaping and dancing before Jehovah, and despised him in her heart. והיה, “and it came to pass,” for ויהי, because there is no progress made, but only another element introduced. בּא is a perfect: “the ark had come, ... and Michal looked through the window, ... there she saw,” etc. Michal is intentionally designated the daughter of Saul here, instead of the wife of David, because on this occasion she manifested her father’s disposition rather than her husband's. In Saul’s time people did not trouble themselves about the ark of the covenant (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.3">1Ch 13:3</reference>); public worship was neglected, and the soul for vital religion had died out in the family of the king. Michal possessed teraphim, and in David she only loved the brave hero and exalted king: she therefore took offence at the humility with which the king, in his pious enthusiasm, placed himself on an equality with all the rest of the nation before the Lord.
entries.96936bee2db6a6806ceddf627a2188472a071462: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17">2Sa 6:17</reference> <div eID="gen4313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4314" type="x-p"/> When the ark was brought to the place appointed for it upon Mount Zion, and was deposited in the tent which David had prepared for it, he offered burnt-offerings and thank-offerings before the Lord. “In its place” is still further defined as “in the midst of the tent which David,” etc., i.e., in the Most Holy Place; for the tent would certainly be constructed according to the type of the Mosaic tabernacle. The burnt-offerings and peace-offerings were offered to consecrate the newly erected house of God.
entries.fb39a2892eef77c228551668009070711a779fbe: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.18-2Sam.6.19">2Sa 6:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen4314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4315" type="x-p"/> When the offering of sacrifice was over, David blessed the people in the name of the Lord, as Solomon did afterwards at the dedication of the temple (1Ki 8:55), and gave to all the (assembled) people, both men and women, to every one a slice of bread, a measure (of wine), and a cake for a festal meal, i.e., for the sacrificial meal, which was celebrated with the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> after the offering of the sacrifices, and after the king had concluded the liturgical festival with a benediction. לחם חלּת is a round cake of bread, baked for sacrificial meals, and synonymous with כּכּר־לחם   (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.3">1Ch 16:3</reference>), as we may see from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Exod.29.23">Exo 29:23</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lev.8.26">Lev 8:26</reference> (see the commentary on <reference osisRef="Lev.8.2">Lev 8:2</reference>). But the meaning of the ἁπ. λεγ. אשׁפּר is uncertain, and has been much disputed. Most of the Rabbins understand it as signifying a piece of flesh or roast meat, deriving the word from אשׁ and פּר; but this is certainly false. There is more to be said in favour of the derivation proposed by L. de Dieu, viz., from the Ethiopic שׁפר, <hi type="italic">netiri</hi>, from which <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Roediger</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> Thes. p. 1470) have drawn their explanation of the word as signifying a measure of wine or other beverage. For אשׁישׁה, the meaning grape-cake or raisin-cake is established by Son of Sol 2:5 and Hos 3:1 (vid., <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>, Christol. on Hos 3:1). The people returned home after the festal meal.
entries.1fca935fbeccc54bb2bc4bc0fa7c4e097c81a1e9: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">2Sa 6:20</reference> <div eID="gen4315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4316" type="x-p"/> When David returned home to bless his house, as he had previously blessed the people, Michal came to meet him with scornful words, saying, <hi type="italic">“How has the king of Israel glorified himself to-day, when he stripped himself before the eyes of the maids of his servants, as only one of the loose people strips himself!”</hi> The unusual combination נגלות כּהגּלות is explained by <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> (§240, <hi type="italic">e</hi>., p. 607) in this manner, that whilst, so far as the sense of the clause is concerned, the second verb ought to be in the infinitive absolute, they were both written with a very slight change of form in the infinitive construct; whereas others regard נגלות as an unusual form of the infinitive absolute (Ges<hi type="italic">.</hi> <hi type="italic">Lehrgeb</hi>. p. 430), or a copyist’s error for נגלה (Thenius, Olsh. <hi type="italic">Gr</hi>. p. 600). The proud daughter of Saul was offended at the fact, that the king had let himself down on this occasion to the level of the people. She availed herself of the shortness of the priests’ shoulder-dress, to make a contemptuous remark concerning David’s dancing, as an impropriety that was unbecoming in a king. “Who knows whether the proud woman did not intend to sneer at the rank of the Levites, as one that was contemptible in her eyes, since their humble service may have looked very trivial to her?” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible.</hi>)
entries.5630b514b0ed479e2a824d2b579fee476fc8f251: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.21-2Sam.6.22">2Sa 6:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen4316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> David replied, “Before Jehovah, who chose me before thy father and all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of Jehovah, over Israel, before Jehovah have I played (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. joked, given utterance to my joy). And I will be still more despised, and become base in my eyes: and with the maidens of whom thou hast spoken, with them will I be honoured.” The copula <hi type="italic">vav</hi> before שׂהקתּי serves to introduce the apodosis, and may be explained in this way, that the relative clause appended to “before Jehovah” acquired the power of a protasis on account of its length; so that, strictly speaking, there is an anakolouthon, as if the protasis read thus: “Before Jehovah, as He hath chosen me over Israel, I have humbled myself before Jehovah” (for “before him”). With the words “who chose me before <hi type="italic">thy father and all his house</hi>,” David humbles the pride of the king’s daughter. His playing and dancing referred to the Lord, who had chosen him, and had rejected Saul on account of his pride. He would therefore let himself be still further despised before the Lord, i.e., would bear still greater contempt from men than that which he had just received, and be humbled in his own eyes (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1">Psa 131:1</reference>): then would he also with the maidens attain to honour before the Lord. For whoso humbleth himself, him will God exalt (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.12">Mat 23:12</reference>). בּעיני is not to be altered into בּעיניך, as in the lxx. This alteration has arisen from a total misconception of the nature of true humility, which is of no worth in its own eyes. The rendering given by De Wette is at variance with both the grammar and the sense (“with the maidens, ... with them will I magnify myself”); and so also is that of Thenius (“with them will I be honoured, i.e., indemnify myself for thy foolish contempt!”).
entries.677b3951b9e35d0ecce5bfbf62a764a595984fd7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.23">2Sa 6:23</reference> <div eID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4318" type="x-p"/> Michael was humbled by God for her pride, and remained childless to the time of her death. David’s Resolution to Build a Temple. The Promised Perpetuity of His Throne - 2 Samuel 7 <div eID="gen4318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> To the erection of a sanctuary for the ark upon Mount Zion there is appended an account of David’s desire to build a temple for the Lord. We find this not only in the text before us, but also in the parallel history in 1 Chron 17. When David had acquired rest from his enemies round about, he formed the resolution to build a house for the Lord, and this resolution was sanctioned by the prophet Nathan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.1-2Sam.7.3">2Sa 7:1-3</reference>). But the Lord revealed to the prophet, and through him to David, that He had not required the building of a temple from any of the tribes of Israel, and that He would first of all build a house himself for His servant David, and confirm the throne to his seed for ever, and then he should build Him a temple (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.4-2Sam.7.17">2Sa 7:4-17</reference>). David then gave utterance to his thanksgiving for this glorious promise in a prayer, in which he praised the unmeasurable grace of God, and prayed for the fulfilment of this renewed promised of divine grace (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.29">2Sa 7:18-29</reference>).<note placement="foot">With regard to the historical authenticity of this promise, Tholuck observes, in his <hi type="italic">Prophets and their Prophecies</hi> (pp. 165-6), that “it can be proved, with all the evidence which is ever to be obtained in support of historical testimony, that David actually received a prophetic promise that his family should sit upon the throne for ever, and consequently an intimation of a royal descendant whose government should be eternal. Anything like a merely subjective promise arising from human combinations is precluded here by the fact that Nathan, acting according to the best of his knowledge, gave his consent to David’s plan of building a temple; and that it was not till afterwards, when he had been instructed by a divine vision, that he did the very opposite, and assured him on the contrary that God would build <hi type="italic">him</hi> a house.” Thenius also affirms that “there is no reason for assuming, as De Wette has done, that Nathan’s prophecies were not composed till after the time of Solomon;” that “their historical credibility is attested by Ps 89 (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.4">Psa 89:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.5">Psa 89:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.20-Ps.89.38">20-38</reference>, and especially <reference osisRef="Ps.89.20">Psa 89:20</reference>), <reference osisRef="Ps.132.11-Ps.132.12">Psa 132:11-12</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference>; and that, properly interpreted, they are also Messianic.” The principal evidence of this is to be found in the prophetic utterance of David in 2 Samuel 23, where, as is generally admitted, he takes a retrospective glance at the promise, and thereby attests the historical credibility of Nathan’s prophecy (Thenius, p. 245). Nevertheless, Gust. Baur maintains that “a closer comparison of this more elaborate and simple description (2 Samuel 7) with the brief and altogether unexampled <hi type="italic">last words of David</hi>, more especially with <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>, can hardly leave the slightest doubt, that the relation in which the chapter before us stands to these words, is that of a later expansion to an authentic prophetic utterance of the king himself.” For example, the distinct allusion to the birth of Solomon, and the building of the temple, which was to be completed by him, is said to have evidently sprung from a later development of the original promise after the time of Solomon, on account of the incongruity apparent in Nathan’s prediction between the ideal picture of the Israelitish monarchy and the definite allusion to Solomon’s building of the temple. But there is no such “incongruity” in Nathan’s prediction; it is only to be found in the naturalistic assumptions of Baur himself, that the utterances of the prophets contained nothing more than subjective and <hi type="italic">ideal</hi> hopes of the future, and not supernatural predictions. This also applies to Diestel’s opinion, that the section <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.4-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:4-16</reference> does not harmonize with the substance of David’s glorious prayer in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.29">2Sa 7:18-29</reference>, nor the latter again with itself, because the advice given him to relinquish the idea of building the temple is not supported by any reasons that answer either to the character of David or to his peculiar circumstances, with which the allusion to his son would have been in perfect keeping; but the prophet’s dissuasion merely alludes to the fact that Jehovah did not stand in need of a stately house at all, and had never given utterance to any such desire. On account of this “obvious” fact, Diestel regards it as credible that the original dissuasion came from God, because it was founded upon an earlier view, but that the promise of the son of David which followed proceeded from Nathan, who no doubt looked with more favourable eyes upon the building of the temple. This discrepancy is also arbitrarily foisted upon the text. There is not a syllable about any “original dissuasion” in all that Nathan says; for he simply tells the king that Jehovah had hitherto dwelt in a tent, and had not asked any of the tribes of Israel to build a stately temple, but not that Jehovah did not need a stately house at all.</note> <div eID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4320" type="x-p"/> Of the different exegetical treatises upon this passage, see <hi type="italic">Christ. Aug. Crusii Hypomnemata</hi>, ii. 190-219, and Hengstenberg’s <hi type="italic">Christol</hi>. i. 123ff.  <chapter eID="2Sam.6"/> <div eID="gen4320" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>AGain David gathered together all <ns0:hi>the</ns0:hi> chosen <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> of Israel <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The stoutest, and valiantest Men in his Army and Land; lest the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> should attempt to disturb them in this work.</ns0:note>, thirty thousand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 13. 5, 6.</ns0:note> David arose, and went with all the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">With the whole body of the People: for these seem to be a differing Party from the 30000 now mentioned. See 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 1, 2.</ns0:note>, from Baale of Judah <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> How <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> it, when they went to it; as is evident, both from 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 6. and because the Ark was there, and to be fetched thence? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Some Affirm, That the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Praeposition <ns0:hi>Mem,</ns0:hi> sometimes sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies <ns0:hi>to,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 11. But there is no need of that: for, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 6. mentions their going to <ns0:hi>Baalah;</ns0:hi> and this place mentions their going from it; and the one of these doth manifestly suppose the other: for they went thither, that they might return thence. So the sence is plain, They <ns0:hi>went from Baaleh of Iudah,</ns0:hi> to bring (or rather to <ns0:hi>carry;</ns0:hi> for the Word signifies either) <ns0:hi>up from thence the ark.</ns0:hi> Where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by it is supposed, that they first went thither, which is rela<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 3. 6. Moreover, this place is commonly called <ns0:hi>Kiriath-jearim,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 1. and 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 5. and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />merly, <ns0:hi>Kiriath-baal, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 15. 60. and <ns0:hi>Baalah, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 15. 9. and here <ns0:hi>Baale of Iudah,</ns0:hi> so called, because it was in the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> as is evident from <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 15. 1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, to bring up from thence the ark of God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Unto <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which in many respects was fit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter for it than <ns0:hi>Baalah;</ns0:hi> because this was a more Publick place, where it would be more observed and regarded; and in the Center of the Kingdom, to which they might more easily come from all parts; and the Royal City, where it might be always at hand for <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to enquire at, as oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion required; and the place which God had allotted for it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> on which the name, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the name of the LORD of hosts was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led upon.</ns0:note> whose name is called by the name of the LORD of hosts <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Thus <ns0:hi>whose,</ns0:hi> belongs not to the <ns0:hi>Ark,</ns0:hi> but to <ns0:hi>God:</ns0:hi> for what follows is not the name of the Ark, but of God. The place may well be, and is by some rendred thus, <ns0:hi>Upon</ns0:hi> (or <ns0:hi>At,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Beside,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Before,) which</ns0:hi> (Ark) <ns0:hi>the name,</ns0:hi> even <ns0:hi>the name of the Lord of hosts, that dwelleth between the Cherubims is called upon: i. e.</ns0:hi> By, or before which, they were to present their Prayers to God for Counsel and Suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cour upon all occasions. And this is mentioned here as the reason why <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> put himself and his people to so great trouble and charge, because it was to fetch up the choicest Treasure which they had, and so the benefit would abun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dantly recompence the inconvenience.</ns0:note>, that dwelleth <ns0:hi>between</ns0:hi> the cherubims.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:251" />3 And they <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> made to ride</ns0:note> set the ark of God <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 1 Sam. 6. 7.</ns0:note> upon a new cart <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Being taught, and encouraged to do so, by the Exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> who did so without any token of Gods displeasure upon them for so doing. But they did not sufficiently consider, that God might wink at the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> because they were ignorant of God's Laws; and yet be an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gry with them for the same thing, because they knew, or might, and should have known the Law of God, which commanded the Priests to bear it upon their shoulders, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 4. 14, 15. and 7. 9. But their present transports of Joy at the happy Change of their Affairs, and their greedy desire of having the Ark removed, made them hasty and inconsiderate.</ns0:note>, and brought it out of the house of Abina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dab that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> the hill.</ns0:note> Gibeah <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>on the hill,</ns0:hi> as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 1.</ns0:note>: and Uzzah and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> his bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther. So Gr.</ns0:note> Ahio the sons of Abinadab <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>Abinadab</ns0:hi> himself seems now to have been dead; or at least, detained at home through infirmity or indispensable oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casions.</ns0:note>, drave the new cart.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And they brought it out of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 7. 1.</ns0:note> the house of Abinadab which <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> at Gibeah, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> with</ns0:note> accompanying the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To lead the Oxen that drew it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And David and all the house of Israel play<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed before the LORD, on all manner of <ns0:hi>instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments made of</ns0:hi> fir-wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 13. 9.</ns0:note> when they came to Nachons <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Otherwise called <ns0:hi>Chidon,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 9.</ns0:note> thresh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing floor, Uzzah <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Num. 4. 15.</ns0:note> put forth <ns0:hi>his hand</ns0:hi> to the ark of God, and took hold of it, for the oxen <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> stumbled, or, threw it down; 2 King. 9. 33.</ns0:note> shook it <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For they stumbled, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God smote him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">With some deadly Disease or Stroke, as it follows.</ns0:note> there for <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> rashness.</ns0:note> errour <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either, 1. For his touching the Ark, when he was no <ns0:hi>Levite,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> reports; nor indeed was <ns0:hi>Kiriath-jearim</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Levitical</ns0:hi> City: or, that being but a <ns0:hi>Levite,</ns0:hi> he touched the bare Ark, which onely the Priests might do, <ns0:hi>Numb</ns0:hi> 4. 15. and 18. 3. And though the Ark was ordinarily cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red, yet it is not impossible but the covering might be ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther loose, and so blown aside by the Wind; or worn out, and so he might touch the Ark it self. Or, 2. Because he put the Ark into a Cart, and thereby exposed it to the dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger of falling, which would have been a great discourage<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and a reproach to the Ark. And though <ns0:hi>Ahio</ns0:hi> also might have an hand in putting it into the Cart, yet <ns0:hi>Uzzah</ns0:hi> onely is smitten; either, because he was the Elder Brother, and the person to whose care the Ark was more especially committed; or, because he was the chief Author of this counsel of putting it into a Cart; or, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he added a new fault of touching the Ark, and that out of distrust of God's care over it.</ns0:note>, and there he died <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This may seem very severe, considering that his Intention was pious, and his Transgression not great. But, besides that, Men are ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry improper Judges of the Actions of God; and that Gods Judgements are always just, though sometimes obscure: there are many things to be said of this, and such like ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses. 1. That it is fit and reasonable, that God should make some persons Examples of his just and high Displeasure against Sins, seemingly small; partly, for the demonstration of his own exact and impartial Holiness; partly, for the Establish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of Discipline, (for which very reason, even Earthly Princes have oft-times Inflicted great Punishments for small Offences;) and for the greater Terrour and Caution of Mankind, who are very prone to have slight thoughts of Sin, and to give way to small Sins, and thereby to be led on to greater; all which is, or may be prevented by such instan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of Severity: and consequently, there is more of God's Mercy, than of his Justice, in such Actions, because the Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice is consined to one particular person, but the Mercy and benefit of it publick and common to Mankind of that, and all future Ages. 2. That God is justly most severe in those things which immediately concern his Worship and Service; and against those persons who have the nearest Relation to him, and the greatest opportunities of Knowing, and the highest obligations of careful Practising those Duties which they neglect: See <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 10. 3. 3. That this Pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishment possibly was not so great, as it may seem to be; for as for his Body, the Disease, though dangerous, might not be exceedingly painful: and for his Soul, the stroke proba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly was not so sudden, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> not to give him space of Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pentance.</ns0:note> by the ark of God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And David was displeased <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>grieved,</ns0:hi> both for the sin, which he acknowledgeth, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 15. 2, 13. and for Gods heavy Judgment; whereby their hopes were dashed, and their joys interrupted, and a good subject struck dead for the circumstantial error of a Pious mind, which he might possibly think harsh and very severe, and therefore be displeased or offended at this sharp Providence.</ns0:note>, because the LORD had <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> had broken.</ns0:note> made a breach uppon Uzzah: And he called the name of the place <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, the breach of <ns0:hi>Uzzah.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Perez Uzzah to this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And David was afraid of the LORD <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either, that God was displeased with him for removing the Ark, and bringing it to his City: or lest God should pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceed further in the way of his Judgments upon him and his people: or, lest the Ark being brought to his House, might be the occasion of inconveniencies and great calamities for some neglects or errors which they might easily and frequently commit.</ns0:note> that day, and said, How shall the ark of the LORD come unto me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">How may I presume, or how shall I dare do it, when God hath shewed his displeasure for my attempting it? I will therefore wait further upon God for his direction in the case, and at present forbear. But why did not <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> consult God presently by the <ns0:hi>Urim,</ns0:hi> as he used to do? This therefore seems to have been his infirmity and neglect.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 So David would not remove the ark of the LORD unto him into the city of David<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but David carried it aside into the house of Obed-Edom <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which doubtless was done by the consent and desire of the owner of it, who for the enjoyment of so great a Pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viledge, was willing to expose himself to some hazard; and wisely considered, that the late Judgment was not to be impu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted to the Ark, but to <ns0:hi>Uzzah</ns0:hi>'s carelesness in managing it.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 21. 24 1 Chr. 13. 13.</ns0:note> Gittite <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He was certainly a <ns0:hi>Levite,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 15. 18, 21, 24. and 16. 5. and 26. 4. and here called a <ns0:hi>Gittite,</ns0:hi> Either, First, From <ns0:hi>Gath</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> where he or his Father might be Born or have Sojourned, which might be upon divers occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions: Or, Secondly, From <ns0:hi>Gath-rimmon,</ns0:hi> which was a <ns0:hi>Le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vitical</ns0:hi> City, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 21. 24, 25.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And the ark of the LORD continued in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite three months: and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom, and all his houshold <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">With happy Success in all their Affairs and Actions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 ¶ And it was told king David, saying, The LORD hath blessed the house of Obed-Edom, and all that <ns0:hi>pertaineth</ns0:hi> unto him, because of the ark of God. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 15. 25.</ns0:note> So David went and brought up the ark of God <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Understanding that the Ark was entertained without danger or inconvenience, and with great advantage, he ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehended his former mistake, and brought it to himself.</ns0:note> from the house of Obed-Edom <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which is thought to have been either in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> or ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry near it.</ns0:note>, into the city of David, with gladness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And it was <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> that when they that bare the ark of the LORD, had gone six paces <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">With safety and comfort.</ns0:note>, he sacri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficed <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 1 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 15. 26.</ns0:note> oxen and fatlings <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Upon an Altar suddenly erected, as was usual in such cases. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 24. This he did, either, to appease God for the former miscarriage: or, to praise him for his present mercy, that he had not made another breach upon them: or, to implore his favour and gracious presence with them in this great Affair.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And David danced before the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To express his inward joy and thankfulness to God by his outward carriage, according to the manner of those times. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15. 20. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 34. and 21. 21. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 18. 6. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 149. 3. and 150. 4.</ns0:note> with all <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> might, and David <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> girded with a linen ephod <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The usual Habit of the Priests and <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> in their Sacred Ministrations, yet some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times worn by others, as it was by the young Child <ns0:hi>Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />muel,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 18. before he was come to those years in which the <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> were allowed to Minister; and so hereby <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> who laid by his Royal Robes, and put on this Robe to signify and declare, that although he was King of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> yet he willingly owned himself to be the Lords Minister and Servant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:251" />15 So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Sauls daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As one of a base and mean spirit, that knew not how to carry himself with that Majesty which became his place, but behaved himself like one of the Fools or vain Persons in <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 16. 1.</ns0:note> they brought in the ark of the LORD, and set it in his place, in the midst of the tabernacle that David had † pitched for it <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Tabernacle was still at <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16. 39. and 21. 29. and 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 1. 3. which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> left there, because he designed to build a Temple at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> with all speed, though he was countermanded therein by God himself.</ns0:note>: and<ns0:note place="margin">‡ <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> stretch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> David offered burnt-offerings, and peace-offerings before the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And assoon as David had made an end of offering burnt-offerings, and peace-offerings, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 16. 2.</ns0:note> he blessed the people <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He heartily and solemnly prayed to God for his Blessing upon them: which he did both as Prophet, and as their King, to whom by office it belongs, by all means, to seek his Peoples welfare.</ns0:note> in the name of the LORD of hosts.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And he dealt among all the people, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> among the whole multitude of Israel, as well to the women as men, to every one a cake of bread, and a good piece <ns0:hi>of flesh,</ns0:hi> and a flaggon <ns0:hi>of wine:</ns0:hi> so all the people departed every one to his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 ¶ Then David returned to bless his house<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold: and Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either, First, by stripping himself of his Royal Robes, that he might put on a <ns0:hi>Levitical</ns0:hi> Ephod: or, by discovering some part of his Thighs or Legs, as might possibly happen whilst <ns0:hi>he danced with all his might,</ns0:hi> as is said above <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14. considering that the men did then wear loose Garments. Or, she speaks thus, not that he did so, but onely by way of aggravation of his fault, and to vilify him the more, as is usual with persons in such cases.</ns0:note> to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Who either bare a part in the Solemnity, as Women sometimes did, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15. 20. or, at least were spectators of it, and of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s carriage in it.</ns0:note>, as one of the vain fellows <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As idle and light persons use to do.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> openly.</ns0:note> shamefully uncovereth himself!</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And David said unto Michal, <ns0:hi>It was</ns0:hi> before the LORD <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In his presence and service, which though contemptible to thee, is, and ever shall be honourable in mine eyes.</ns0:note>, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which took away the honour from him and his, and trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferred it upon me, whereby he hath obliged me to Love and Serve him with all my might.</ns0:note>, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I will always be ready to humble and abase my self be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore God.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>andmaids <ns0:hi>of my servants.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">I shall rather chuse to get honour from the meanest of my people, in serving and praising God, than to gain esteem from thee by my lukewarmness in Gods ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Therefore <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not because of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s words to her, which have no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing in them to this purpose; but because of her proud, and petulant, and ungodly speech and carriage to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> which God justly punished with sterility.</ns0:note> Michal the daughter of Saul had no child <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To wit, by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and after this time, which these words evidently respect. Which was true, although those five Children ascribed to <ns0:hi>Michal,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 8. were hers by Birth, and not by Adoption onely.</ns0:note> until the day of her death <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Never: for if she ever had any, it must be before her death. Compare 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 15. 35. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 1. 25.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
